The counter ran along the left side of the hall, scarred oak polished dark by decades of elbows. Behind it sat a thin woman of middle years with ink-stained fingers and spectacles perched low on her nose, copying entries into a ledger. She finished her line before she looked up. "Registration." Not a question. She set the quill down in its holder and pulled a fresh sheet toward her. "Name?" He gave it, and she wrote it out in a small, even hand. "Alaric Red. Human, Mage." Her eyes flicked once over the staff and robes, cataloguing rather than judging. "Right. The way it works: registration costs two silver, one-time. Separate thing from your power rank, that's what you are strength-wise, and the measuring stone reads that on its own. We don't grant that, we just write down what it says." She turned the sheet toward him, tapping a blank space at the bottom with one ink-stained finger. "Two silver, sign there, and you're in the book. No fee, no registration — house rule, not mine." She said it without apology, already reaching for the blotting sand.

The board stood hip-high and crowded, papers pinned four and five deep, some so old the ink had gone brown. Most were beyond him on sight — the clerk's rule was plain enough in the way the higher postings carried wax seals and coloured ribbons where the low ones carried none. He picked through the plain white slips near the bottom, the ones marked for Novices, and read while the hall's morning noise washed around him: boots, the clerk's quill, somebody laughing too loud by the map table. There was real work on offer, all of it the unglamorous kind. Boars to be culled along the old quarry track east of the city, four of them, for a hundred and twenty copper from the carters' cooperative. Snakes thinning at the millpond sluice works, three kills, ninety-five copper, posted by the pond's own keeper. A charcoal burner named Brenna Hollis wanted five grey wolves dead at her camp in the coppice north of the quarry track, a hundred and fifty copper for the lot. The reed-cutters of the Ditch Marsh had a single beast troubling their causeway — a marsh raptor, one kill, a hundred and seventy-five copper, the richest of the paper slips. And pinned last, on stiffer stock with the Guild's own stamp, a dungeon job: clear the first level of the Mossback Warrens, a hundred and forty copper, with a warning in the text itself about groups and stronger foes and no promise that a matching rank made a solo expedition safe. He thanked the carter and went down the bank with the staff in one hand, testing the first stone with the toe of his boot before committing weight to it. It held. The water pulled at his ankles just short of his knees, cold enough to bite through the cloth, and he stood a moment and let the current's push tell him what he was dealing with. The second stone sat deeper in shadow, slick with weed. He got a foot onto it and the staff's end down into the water for balance, and for three heartbeats it worked — one step, then another, halfway out now, the carter and the dog both watching from the bank. Then the third stone shifted under him. Not much. An inch, a grinding roll of it, but enough. His back foot skated off the wet top, arms went wide, the staff slapped sideways into the current, and he came down hard across the stone's edge — hip and forearm taking the impact before the water closed over him to the chest. The stream shoved at him like something alive. He got a hand onto the fourth stone and dragged himself half out, coughing, one leg still in the pull of it, then hauled himself back onto the near bank on hands and knees. His forearm had taken a scrape the length of it, raw and bleeding freely, and his hip throbbed where the stone's edge had caught him; water ran out of his clothes and pooled under him in the dust. The staff was still in his grip — he'd never let go of it — dripping brown. "Stones have gone, then," the carter said, not unkindly, coming a few steps nearer. "Told you they'd shifted. You all right?" The dog trotted over, sniffed at the wet hem, and sat. The ford stayed as it had been: brown, quick, and between him and the mossy hill.

The water pulled at his ankles just short of his knees, cold enough to bite through the cloth, and he stood a moment and let the current's push tell him what he was dealing with.

The second stone sat deeper in shadow, slick with weed. He got a foot onto it and the staff's end down into the water for balance, and for three heartbeats it worked — one step, then another, halfway out now, the carter and the dog both watching from the bank. Then the third stone shifted under him. Not much. An inch, a grinding roll of it, but enough. His back foot skated off the wet top, arms went wide, the staff slapped sideways into the current, and he came down hard across the stone's edge — hip and forearm taking the impact before the water closed over him to the chest.

The stream shoved at him like something alive. He got a hand onto the fourth stone and dragged himself half out, coughing, one leg still in the pull of it, then hauled himself back onto the near bank on hands and knees. His forearm had taken a scrape the length of it, raw and bleeding freely, and his hip throbbed where the stone's edge had caught him; water ran out of his clothes and pooled under him in the dust. The staff was still in his grip — he'd never let go of it — dripping brown.

"Stones have gone, then," the carter said, not unkindly, coming a few steps nearer. "Told you they'd shifted. You all right?" The dog trotted over, sniffed at the wet hem, and sat.

The ford stayed as it had been: brown, quick, and between him and the mossy hill.

He went back to pacing by his cart, and the dog watched Alaric wring out a boot before sitting again in the sun. His hip kept a dull complaint with every step, and his boots squelched, but the sun was warm and the walk west would dry him as it went. The carter gave him a lift of two fingers off his brow as he climbed back up to the track. The fork came where the carter had said, a split in the track with a grey post leaning at it, the rag on top bleached and half-torn. The narrower way led off through birch and alder, the ground going soft underfoot, and after a few hundred paces the trees opened on the narrows — a place where the stream pinched between mossy banks and ran quieter, glassy over dark stones. The footbridge was a single peeled log laid bank to bank, handrails of rope at two heights gone grey and hairy, one staked and one sagging loose. It had been a decent bridge once. Now the bark had worn off in the middle where feet had polished it, and nearer the far end a length of the wood had gone pale and fibrous where rot had moved in, a soft-looking span of maybe two paces with a dark split running down its crown. The log itself was thick enough — wider than a boot — and the drop below was only a few feet of water, shallow over stones, but the current looked quicker on this side than the ford's had been, funneled between the banks. The first part of the crossing was easy enough — dry log, rope rail holding taut at his hip, the water sliding glass-slow beneath. He kept his weight low and his eyes on his feet, and the polished middle passed under his boots fine. The rot announced itself too late. His heel came down on the pale span and the wood gave with a wet, fibrous crunch, splitting along its dark seam, and the whole length of it sagged under him like old bread. He grabbed for the rope rail — his hand closed on it, held — but his leg went through to the knee, and the rough broken edge of the log raked down his shin as he dragged himself back onto solid wood. Splinters, a hot stinging line of them, blood welling slow through the scrape. He got both feet under him on the sound part of the bridge and stood there breathing, one hand still on the rope, while the broken span swayed and dripped below him. He went the rest of the way straddled, half sitting, moving hand over hand along the rail, and dropped off onto the far bank mud with his heart going hard. His shin burned. His hip from the ford had company now. The bridge behind him had lost its middle — the broken span hung from the rail-stakes, useless — and this side of the stream was not the side he'd started on. The rest of the way he walked wet-booted and slow. The birch ground rose, gave over to gorse and bracken, and the old quarry track found him again east of the ford, running up toward the wooded hills. Somewhere past midday the trees closed overhead and the air went cool and mushroom-damp, and then the land swelled up green and there it was. The moss-grown hill sat off the track's end like a thing sleeping. Grass and moss ran thick up its flanks, broken by dark stooping shapes — weathered standing stones in a ring around its base, lichened grey-green, some fallen. And on the near side, at the ring's center, a gap in the hillside itself: a doorway of leaning slabs opening into a passage that went down into the dark, cold air breathing out of it, smelling of wet earth and something older. Mossback Warrens. No sound came up out of it. His shin throbbed, and the hill waited.

The first part of the crossing was easy enough — dry log, rope rail holding taut at his hip, the water sliding glass-slow beneath. He kept his weight low and his eyes on his feet, and the polished middle passed under his boots fine.

The rot announced itself too late. His heel came down on the pale span and the wood gave with a wet, fibrous crunch, splitting along its dark seam, and the whole length of it sagged under him like old bread. He grabbed for the rope rail — his hand closed on it, held — but his leg went through to the knee, and the rough broken edge of the log raked down his shin as he dragged himself back onto solid wood. Splinters, a hot stinging line of them, blood welling slow through the scrape. He got both feet under him on the sound part of the bridge and stood there breathing, one hand still on the rope, while the broken span swayed and dripped below him.

He went the rest of the way straddled, half sitting, moving hand over hand along the rail, and dropped off onto the far bank mud with his heart going hard. His shin burned. His hip from the ford had company now. The bridge behind him had lost its middle — the broken span hung from the rail-stakes, useless — and this side of the stream was not the side he'd started on.

The rest of the way he walked wet-booted and slow. The birch ground rose, gave over to gorse and bracken, and the old quarry track found him again east of the ford, running up toward the wooded hills. Somewhere past midday the trees closed overhead and the air went cool and mushroom-damp, and then the land swelled up green and there it was.

The moss-grown hill sat off the track's end like a thing sleeping. Grass and moss ran thick up its flanks, broken by dark stooping shapes — weathered standing stones in a ring around its base, lichened grey-green, some fallen. And on the near side, at the ring's center, a gap in the hillside itself: a doorway of leaning slabs opening into a passage that went down into the dark, cold air breathing out of it, smelling of wet earth and something older. Mossback Warrens.

No sound came up out of it. His shin throbbed, and the hill waited.

The word left him and the wave went with it — a ring of pale force that slapped off the mossy walls and struck all three where they stood. The air shivered. The two squabblers were knocked back a half-step, hides seared grey where it caught them; the one that had seen him first took it across the chest and its shriek broke into a cough. All three lived through it, and all three came on. They were quick. The big-eared one reached him first, knife low, and drove it into his thigh — a jag of cold fire that folded his knee. The second was on him before he could bring the staff around, its knife worrying at his side, once, twice, hot blood spilling over his hip where the ford's scrape was. The third came in behind them both, jabbing at his arm, cutting him down between the shoulders as he sagged. The staff clattered on stone. The chamber's crack of grey light went on shining on the moss above them, indifferent. Somewhere in him the cold of the passage won, and his breath thinned to nothing, and the wet grass smell and the musk and the trickle of water were the last of the world. The three goblins stood over the body, panting, jabbering low. The big-eared one prodded him once with a foot, then straightened and looked toward the passage mouth, ears swiveling — listening for whatever else the shriek might have woken.
